Modeling and Forecasting Tail Risk Spillovers:
A Component-Based CAViaR Approach
Demetrio Lacava∗
Department of Economics, University of Messina, Messina, v ia
dei Verdi, 75, 98122, Italy.
Abstract
This paper introduces a new extension of the Conditional Au-
toregressive Value at Risk (CAViaR) model aimed at improvin g tail
risk forecasting across assets. The proposed component-ba sed model,
CAViaR with Spillover Eﬀects (CAViaR-SE), decomposes the co n-
ditional Value at Risk into a proper-risk component and a spi llover
component driven by a linear combination of tail risks from i nﬂuential
assets. These assets are selected via a recursive partial co rrelation al-
gorithm, allowing multiple spillover sources with minimal parameteri-
zation. The spillover component acts as a predictable quant ile shifter,
directly aﬀecting the conditional quantile dynamics rather than the
volatility scale. Empirical results on Dow Jones Industria l Average
stocks show that spillover eﬀects account for a substantial s hare of to-
tal tail risk and signiﬁcantly improve out-of-sample tail r isk forecasts.
Backtesting procedures, together with Model Conﬁdence Set (MCS)
analysis, conﬁrm that CAViaR-SE provides well-calibrated risk mea-
sures and statistically superior forecasts compared to sta ndard and
augmented CAViaR models.
Keywords: Value at Risk, CAViaR, Spillover eﬀects, inﬂuential assets.

SincetheBaselagreements, ValueatRisk(VaR)andExpected Sho rtfall(ES)
have been considered standard measures for ﬁnancial risk: VaR s ummarizes

description of downside tail risk, making them leading tools for both r isk
management and ﬁnancial regulation. From a risk management pers pective,
these measures are employed to quantify potential losses over a g iven period
(one day, one week, or one month). From a regulatory viewpoint, V aR and
ES represent the basis for the determination of capital requireme nts aimed
at ensuring the stability of the ﬁnancial system, particularly during periods
of market stress.
The literature has proposed three main approaches for the estima tion of
VaR and ES. The non-parametric approach, based on historical da ta with-
out assuming a speciﬁc probability distribution: this ensures a high de gree
of ﬂexibility but makes this approach less suitable for forecasting pu rposes.
Conversely, the parametric approach requires an explicit assumpt ion on the
distribution underlying a volatility model, generally a GARCH-type mode l
(Bollerslev, 1986): VaR is then obtained from the corresponding th eoreti-
cal quantile. While this approach typically provides good forecasting per-
formance, it is highly sensitive to the assumed distributional speciﬁc ation.
Finally, the semi-parametric approach can be viewed as an intermedia te so-
lution between parametric and non-parametric methods. It relies o n a para-
metric speciﬁcation for the conditional dynamics, while allowing for a m ore
ﬂexible modeling of the distribution, particularly in the tails.
Amongthesemi-parametricmodels, theConditionalAutoregressiv eValue
at Risk (CAViaR) model proposed by Engle and Manganelli (2004) has
proven to be eﬀective in capturing the dynamics of the conditional q uan-
tile, with adequate performance both in-sample and out-of-sample . In the
CAViaR framework, the VaR follows an autoregressive structure a ugmented
with anobserved variableaccounting fortheimpact ofthemost rec ent return
on the expected maximum loss. More recently, Mitrodima and Oberoi (2024)
propose an extension of the CAViaR framework that jointly models V aR and
ES through autoregressive tail dynamics, allowing for long-range d ependence
andhorizon-speciﬁc aggregationandimproving tail-riskforecastin g accuracy.
Generally, VaR is constructed relying exclusively on the returns of t he
asset under consideration, typically abstracting from the inﬂuenc e of other
factors. In this regard, the inclusion of overnight returns (Meng and Taylor,
2018) or the High–Low volatility estimator (Chen et al., 2012) in the Va R
process allows to outperform GARCH-based methods and standar d CAViaR
models.1Furthermore, the inclusion of realized measures of volatility im-

proves the VaR predictive ability relative to baseline speciﬁcations, b oth in
the semi-parametric ( ˇZikeˇ s and Barun´ ık, 2015) and in the parametric frame-
work (Brownlees and Gallo, 2010). However, the CAViaR models are g en-
erally built without accounting for the fact that risk can propagate across
assets and markets. It is well known that ﬁnancial markets are hig hly inte-
grated, with strong return correlations among stocks. For insta nce, on May
11, 2012, JPMorgan Chase (JPM) recorded a −10% return after announc-
ing a massive loss stemming from complex credit derivative positions (t he
so-called “London Whale”), while Goldman Sachs (GS) experienced a −4%
decline, despite the absence of ﬁrm-speciﬁc news, suggesting the presence of
downside risk spillovers originating from a single institution.
In this respect, a limited but growing body of research investigates the
propagation of tail risk across markets using tools that explicitly allo w for
linkages at extreme quantiles. These approaches underscore the importance
of modeling tail interdependence directly, beyond second-moment spillover
metrics. For example, Garcia-Jorcano and Sanchis-Marco (2022) propose
a state-dependent model that captures ES spillovers across diﬀe rent mar-
ket conditions (tranquil, normal, and volatile). Spillovers in VaR are als o
analyzed using the so-called Conditional VaR (CoVaR, Adrian and Bru n-
nermeier, 2016; Girardi and Erg¨ un, 2013), which measures the r isk of the
ﬁnancial system, or of a particular asset, conditional on another institution
being in distress. Xi et al. (2025) combine DCC-GARCH models, netwo rk
analysis, and quantile regression to investigate how changes in mark et inter-
connectedness aﬀectVaR,therebycapturingdownsideriskspillov ers. Finally,
Su (2020) applies quantile variance decomposition to measure extre me risk
spillovers by extending the spillover index proposed by Diebold and Yilma z
(2009) within a quantile regression framework.
In this paper, we analyze potential tail risk spillovers by proposing a
new extension of the CAViaR model of Engle and Manganelli (2004), c alled
CAViaR with Spillover Eﬀects (CAViaR-SE). In our speciﬁcation, the c on-
ditional quantile is decomposed into two distinct components captur ing, re-
spectively, the asset’s proper risk dynamics and spillover eﬀects. T he proper-
risk component follows a standard CAViaR speciﬁcation, while the spillo ver
component is modeled as an autoregressive process augmented wit h a proxy
for spillover eﬀects. Importantly, spillovers enter the conditional quantile as
a predictable quantile shifter, rather than through volatility scaling . This
structure allows us to quantify the contribution of spillover-relate d risk to
total tail risk when estimating a CAViaR speciﬁcation with latent fact ors.
The spillover eﬀect is measured by a linear combination of risk measure s as-
sociated with a set of inﬂuential assets that may act as sources of spillover for
the asset under consideration. The set of inﬂuential assets is iden tiﬁed using

the recursive algorithm proposed by Gallo et al. (2025), which select s the
variables exhibiting the highest partial correlation with the asset of interest:
this approach accounts for multiple spillover sources while introducin g only
one additional parameter into the model.
Theempiricalanalysis, basedontheassetsbelongingtotheDowJon esIn-
dustrial Average index, reveals several novel ﬁndings. First, th e identiﬁed set
ofinﬂuential assetssuggests thatspillover eﬀectsreﬂect under lying structural
economicmechanismsratherthanspuriouscorrelations. Second, thespillover
component enters the model with a positive coeﬃcient, indicating th at ex-
treme losses in the selected assets are associated with more sever e losses for
the asset under consideration. Third, the spillover component acc ounts for
the 20% of total tail risk, at least. Fourth, the proposed speciﬁc ation delivers
reliable VaR estimates and successfully passes standard backtest ing proce-
dures. Finally, and most importantly, the CAViaR-SE model preserv es the
simplicity and interpretability of the CAViaR framework, while enhancin g
its ability to forecast tail risk in interconnected markets, as highligh ted by
the out-of-sample forecasting analysis.
The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces the theor etical
framework, with the proposed model and the selection algorithm pr esented
in Sections 2.1–2.2; Section 3 presents the dataset, while Section 4 d iscusses
the estimation results, with the out-of-sample forecast evaluate d in Section
4.1. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper with some ﬁnal remarks.

Risk spillover is the transmission of risk from one asset to one other, with
higher correlated stocks that are likely to be more inﬂuenced each o ther.

5 Final remarks
In this paper, we propose a new class of models to analyze how s pillover eﬀects
impact the dynamics of VaR and ES. In particular, we suggest v ariants of the
standard CAViaR models, called CAViaR with Spillover Eﬀects (CAViaR-SE) in
which the conditional quantile is the sum of two components, one capturing the
contribution of spillover eﬀects, the other reproducing the traditional dynamics of
tail risk. The spillover eﬀect is proxied through a linear com bination of the VaR
of a set of inﬂuential assets (identiﬁed via a recursive sele ction algorithm) that
may act as sources of spillover for the asset under considera tion. Moreover, the
component-based structure of the model allows us to isolate and extract a distinct
signal associated with spillover-driven tail risk.
The empirical application, based on individual stocks from the Dow Jones In-
dustrial Average index, provides evidence of superior perf ormance of the CAViaR-
SE relative to both the standard CAViaR and the CAViaR-X, in w hich the same
spillover proxy enters the model as an exogenous regressor. In particular, the
results highlight that the deﬁnition and modeling of the spi llover component are
crucial for correctly capturing spillover eﬀects and for obt aining well-calibrated
VaR estimates that successfully pass standard backtesting procedures. Further-
more, we ﬁnd that spillover eﬀects account for a substantial f raction of tail risk, as
the share of total risk directly attributable to the spillov er component is at least
20%.

Crucially, the inclusion of the spillover component also im proves out-of-sample
tail risk forecasting performance, as documented by the Mod el Conﬁdence Set
(MCS) results. Finally, theCAViaR-SEis systematically pr eferredwhencompared
with a parametric model in which spillover eﬀects enter the co nditional volatility
dynamics, suggesting that spillovers primarily operate th rough the conditional
quantile dynamics rather than through the scale of the VaR.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This document introduces a new component-based extension of the Conditional Autoregressive Value at Risk (CAViaR) model, called CAViaR with Spillover Effects (CAViaR-SE). The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Standard Value at Risk (VaR) models often overlook the influence of other assets on an asset's tail risk, despite the interconnectedness of financial markets.
*   **Proposed Solution:** The CAViaR-SE model decomposes conditional VaR into two components: a "proper-risk" component (standard CAViaR) and a "spillover" component.
*   **Spillover Component:** This component is driven by a linear combination of tail risks from "influential assets" identified through a recursive partial correlation algorithm. This allows for multiple spillover sources with minimal parameterization.
*   **Mechanism:** The spillover component acts as a predictable quantile shifter, directly impacting the conditional quantile dynamics rather than the volatility scale.
*   **Empirical Findings:** Applied to Dow Jones Industrial Average stocks, the model shows that spillover effects account for a significant portion of total tail risk and substantially improve out-of-sample tail risk forecasts.
*   **Performance:** Backtesting and Model Confidence Set (MCS) analysis confirm that CAViaR-SE provides well-calibrated risk measures and statistically superior forecasts compared to standard and augmented CAViaR models.
*   **Contribution:** The paper aims to enhance tail risk forecasting in interconnected markets while maintaining the simplicity and interpretability of the CAViaR framework.
*   **Background:** The document also provides a review of VaR and Expected Shortfall (ES) as risk measures, discusses different approaches to their estimation (non-parametric, parametric, semi-parametric), and highlights the effectiveness of CAViaR models, along with existing extensions and related literature on tail risk spillovers.

structure.title: Conditional Autoregressive Value at Risk models
structure.summary: This partial document discusses the estimation of Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES). The document details three CAViaR specifications: Symmetric Absolute Value (SAV), Asymmetric Slope (AS), and Indirect GARCH (IG), explaining their mathematical formulations and the interpretation of their parameters. It then introduces Expected Shortfall (ES) as a measure of average loss beyond VaR and presents a parametrization linking ES to CAViaR-based VaR. The document also outlines a joint estimation framework for VaR and ES using a negative log-likelihood function. Finally, it proposes an extension to the CAViaR model, the CAViaR with Spillover Effects (CAViaR-SE), which incorporates a time-varying spillover effect alongside the proper risk dynamics, using the SAV specification as an example.

structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt details a methodology for identifying and analyzing spillover effects among financial assets, likely within the context of Value at Risk (VaR) modeling.

The main points covered are:

*   **A recursive algorithm for selecting influential assets:** This algorithm involves computing correlations, identifying the series with the highest correlation, and iteratively refining a set of influential assets. It aims to avoid arbitrariness associated with parameter choices in other methods like sparse PCA.
*   **Data description:** The empirical application uses daily stock data from the Dow Jones Industrial Average (excluding one ticker) for a specific period.
*   **Cross-quantilogram analysis:** This technique is used to measure quantile dependence, specifically how extreme values in one series predict extreme values in another. The findings suggest positive correlations in tail dependence, indicating that extreme negative returns in one asset are associated with extreme negative returns in another. It also highlights that tail correlation is lower than linear correlation.
*   **Identification of spillover structures:** Table 1 presents the estimated spillover structures, showing how different assets contribute to spillovers. The analysis categorizes assets based on their spillover sources, noting differences between broadly diversified assets (e.g., AMGN, MSFT), financial institutions (e.g., GS, JPM), and assets linked to industrial and financial sectors (e.g., CVX, INTC, WMT).
*   **Empirical application of CAViaR models:** The document mentions estimating baseline CAViaR specifications (SAV, AS, IG) with a specific quantile (τ=0.05). The results indicate high persistence in VaR dynamics and expected relationships between VaR and asset risk/returns.

structure.title: Estimation results
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on the empirical application and evaluation of Conditional Autoregressive Value at Risk (CAViaR) models, particularly in accounting for spillover effects in financial markets.

The main points covered are:

*   **Estimation of CAViaR Models:** The document presents estimation results for baseline CAViaR specifications (SAV, AS, IG) and their extensions that incorporate spillover effects (CAViaR-SE and CAViaR-X).
*   **Persistence of VaR Dynamics:** The estimated VaR dynamics exhibit high persistence across different models and assets, with the autoregressive coefficient ($\hat{\beta}_1$) generally exceeding 0.75.
*   **Interpretation of Model Coefficients:** The signs and significance of coefficients like $\hat{\beta}_2$ and $\hat{\beta}_3$ are discussed in relation to how VaR responds to asset risk and negative returns. The negative $\hat{\gamma}$ coefficient is explained as ensuring a bounded and conservative Expected Shortfall (ES) relative to VaR.
*   **Spillover Effects Analysis:** The document investigates the role of spillover effects, particularly through the $\hat{\phi}_1$ and $\hat{\phi}_2$ coefficients. It notes that spillover effects are often driven by exogenous proxies rather than persistent dynamics. The positive $\hat{\phi}_2$ coefficient suggests that higher expected losses in influential assets lead to more severe extreme losses for the asset being analyzed.
*   **Visualizing Spillover Components:** Figure 2 illustrates the evolution of the spillover component ($q^s_{i,t}$) for selected tickers, highlighting its negative values and downward spikes during major market events and even calm periods, indicating amplification of tail risk due to shocks from other assets.
*   **Contribution of Spillover to Tail Risk:** The analysis quantifies the relative contribution of the spillover component to total tail risk, showing significant variation across assets (e.g., 20% for INTC to 80% for TRV).
*   **Model Misspecification and Backtesting:** Extensive backtesting (Violation Rate, Unconditional Coverage, Conditional Coverage, Dynamic Quantile tests) is performed to evaluate the performance of different models. The CAViaR-X models with negative spillover coefficients are found to be misspecified, failing to meet coverage and independence properties. In contrast, the CAViaR-SE specification is shown to deliver well-calibrated VaR estimates and passes backtesting tests.
*   **Out-of-Sample Evaluation:** The Model Confidence Set (MCS) procedure is used to compare the out-of-sample forecasting performance of the models. The CAViaR-SE specification demonstrates strong and robust forecasting performance, generally outperforming other models.
*   **Conclusion on Spillover Modeling:** The findings strongly suggest that an explicit spillover component is crucial for accurately modeling tail risk dynamics, improving upon volatility-based approaches and highlighting the influence of cross-market interactions on extreme risk.

nodes.title: Out-of-sample forecast
nodes.summary:
This partial document focuses on the out-of-sample evaluation of a new class of models called CAViaR with Spillover Effects (CAViaR-SE) for forecasting Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES). The evaluation uses a rolling-window scheme and the Model Confidence Set (MCS) procedure with the FZ0 loss function. Key findings include:

*   The proposed CAViaR-SE model demonstrates strong and robust forecasting performance across most assets.
*   Augmented CAViaR-X models show more varied performance, with specific variants like SAV-X and AS-X sometimes included in the confidence set.
*   The AS-X specification is identified as the preferred model for JPM and MSFT, even with a negative spillover coefficient in the full-sample analysis, due to the spillover coefficient turning positive in a significant portion of the rolling windows.
*   Baseline CAViaR models, except for the AS specification, generally perform poorly.
*   Directly incorporating spillover effects into the CAViaR specification (as in CAViaR-SE) improves VaR-ES forecasts compared to including them as exogenous regressors (as in SAMEM).
*   The study concludes that the CAViaR-SE model provides reliable out-of-sample forecasts and highlights the importance of the sign, stability, and direct inclusion of the spillover coefficient in the model specification for predictive accuracy.
*   The empirical application suggests that spillover effects account for a substantial fraction of tail risk, at least 20%.

structure.title: Conclusion
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on evaluating the performance of a new class of models called CAViaR with Spillover Effects (CAViaR-SE) for forecasting Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES).

The main points covered are:

*   **Model Confidence Set (MCS) Analysis:** Table 8 presents p-values from the MCS based on the FZ0 loss function for one-step-ahead out-of-sample forecasts. Models within the 0.25 significance level confidence set are highlighted in bold, indicating their superior predictive performance.
*   **CAViaR-SE Model Performance:** The text concludes that the CAViaR-SE model provides reliable out-of-sample VaR-ES forecasts.
*   **Importance of Spillover Effects:** The findings emphasize that the sign and stability of the spillover coefficient, as well as its direct inclusion in the CAViaR specification, are crucial for the predictive accuracy of augmented CAViaR models.
*   **Model Innovation:** The paper introduces CAViaR-SE models that decompose conditional quantiles into a component capturing spillover effects and another representing traditional tail risk dynamics. The spillover effect is proxied by a linear combination of VaRs of influential assets.
*   **Empirical Evidence:** An empirical application using Dow Jones Industrial Average stocks demonstrates that CAViaR-SE outperforms standard CAViaR and CAViaR-X (where spillover proxies are exogenous regressors).
*   **Significance of Spillover Component Modeling:** The results highlight the critical role of defining and modeling the spillover component for accurate spillover capture and well-calibrated VaR estimates.
*   **Contribution of Spillover Risk:** Spillover effects are found to account for a substantial fraction of tail risk, with at least 20% of total risk directly attributable to the spillover component.
*   **Improved Forecasting:** The inclusion of the spillover component enhances out-of-sample tail risk forecasting performance, as confirmed by the MCS results.
*   **Quantile vs. Volatility Dynamics:** The CAViaR-SE model is preferred over parametric models where spillovers affect conditional volatility, suggesting that spillovers primarily influence conditional quantile dynamics.
